pages.search_intent: Classify incoming reference queries into appropriate administrative departments.
pages.summary: Automated routing of digital library reference requests to specialized archival or research teams.
pages.problem: Public library systems receive diverse user queries that often span multiple subjects. Manual sorting results in frequent misrouting of interdisciplinary requests and increased administrative overhead. The application must analyze the query text and provide a consistent department selection to trigger an automated ticketing system update.
pages.input_description: A user-submitted query text string regarding research assistance.
pages.decision: Choice: Map the input to a specific department (e.g., genealogy, digital-media, technical-services) or route to manual review.
pages.action: Downstream code updates the ticketing system status and routes the request to the chosen department queue.

seo.title: Automating Library Reference Query Routing with Intent Classification
seo.description: Learn how to build an automated routing system for library reference requests by classifying user queries into specialized department queues using Choice questions.

pages.intro: Librarians must manually sort incoming reference queries into specialized department queues. This example demonstrates how to automate routing decisions by classifying queries into specific archival or research departments.
pages.solution: The application sends user queries as 'state' and uses the 'dept_routing' Choice question to categorize intent. When the API returns a 'choice' value like 'genealogy' or 'digital_media', your application code interprets the returned string to map the ticket to the corresponding internal database queue. If the API returns 'manual_review', your code can trigger an escalation flow to alert a human librarian. You can implement custom logic to verify the 'confidence' level before taking action, such as automatically routing high-confidence results while holding lower-confidence classifications for secondary review.
limitations: A single Choice question provides only one classification label, though you can support multi-label workflows by defining additional independent questions within the same request.
The API's output is an observed judgment based on provided criteria and does not constitute a rigid guarantee of accuracy for all future inputs.

pages.search_intent: Check whether software license request justifications include a purpose and project reference.
pages.summary: Triage software license requests for missing business context before procurement review.
pages.problem: Software license requests often arrive with vague justifications. A procurement reviewer needs a stated purpose and project reference before checking budget, entitlement and approval rules. This example checks whether the submitted text supplies those two details so the application can request missing information first.
pages.input_description: The 'justification' field submitted in the procurement form.
pages.decision: Noul: Does the justification state a concrete work purpose and include a specific project identifier?
pages.action: Send sufficiently complete requests to procurement review; ask the requester for more detail when the justification is incomplete.

seo.title: Check Software License Justifications Before Procurement Review
seo.description: Use a TypeSafe Noul question to check whether software license requests state a purpose and project reference before sending them to procurement review.

pages.intro: A request such as “I need software for work” leaves a procurement reviewer with little to assess. Use this example to check for a stated work purpose and project reference before starting the approval process.
pages.solution: Send the justification text as state and ask v_01 whether it includes a concrete purpose and a specific project identifier. The primary example supplies both details, while the vague and empty examples do not. Your application can use the returned Noul probability to separate requests that are ready for procurement review from requests that need more information. Choose that threshold using your own labeled examples, then check project records, budget and approval rules separately before granting a license.
limitations: A project identifier in text does not establish that the project exists or is active. Check an authoritative project registry separately.
This request checks the completeness of a justification. It does not establish entitlement, budget availability or procurement approval.
A single Noul answer does not identify which detail is missing. Separate questions can check purpose and project reference individually.

pages.search_intent: Screen raw material specification sheets for undeclared allergen risks.
pages.summary: Triage supplier ingredient specification sheets to flag potential unlabeled common food allergens before inventory intake.
pages.problem: The input provides supplier-submitted ingredient compositions, processing aid descriptions, and facility handling statements. Suppliers use varied phrasing for cross-contact risks, making basic keyword searches prone to confusing trace warnings with active ingredients or omitting unmentioned allergens entirely. The application must classify the text disclosure so downstream services can route ambiguous or incomplete records to specialists for review before intake. This text-based triage evaluates only what the supplier documented; it does not replace independent laboratory testing or authoritative verification of facility sanitation.
pages.input_description: A JSON object containing the supplier ingredient notes, facility handling notes, and stated composition.
pages.decision: Choice: Classify the ingredient profile into allergen-free-declared, allergen-present-declared, ambiguous-trace-warning, or missing-disclosure.
pages.action: Downstream code marks the batch profile for immediate warehouse release, routes it to an allergen specialist for audit, or returns the form to the supplier requesting missing documentation.

seo.title: Screen Ingredient Spec Sheets for Allergen Disclosures
seo.description: Classify supplier ingredient spec sheets to identify allergen declarations, trace warnings, or missing disclosures before inventory intake and manufacturing.

pages.intro: Incoming raw material specification sheets often describe cross-contact risks, processing aids, and facility disclosures in unstructured supplier text. Quality assurance specialists need to triage these statements before materials enter production inventory. This example helps your intake workflow decide whether a supplier specification states clear allergen presence, explicit allergen freedom, ambiguous trace warnings, or incomplete disclosures.
pages.solution: The application supplies raw material specifications containing composition, processing aids, and facility handling notes to evaluate the allergen_triage choice question. In the observed examples, the API returned ambiguous_trace_warning for shared equipment warnings, allergen_free_declared for explicit statements of dedicated allergen-free facilities, and missing_disclosure when facility notes were blank. The API only provides this classification judgment, leaving policy enforcement and execution entirely to your downstream application code. Downstream logic can use these labels to route ambiguous warnings to QA specialists for audit, request updated documents from suppliers on missing disclosures, and hold materials until separate intake verifications are completed.
limitations: Classifying a sheet as allergen_free_declared evaluates only the supplier's self-reported text; it does not confirm facility sanitation, test reports, or regulatory compliance. You can use these triage labels to direct records to the right review queue, but staff or external systems still need to perform independent authoritative checks before granting production approval.

The demonstrated allergen_triage question uses a single Choice primitive that returns only one overall category per evaluation. While this single question does not output a per-allergen breakdown, you can implement separate questions or multi-label workflows if you need to detect distinct individual allergens across the text.

Observed responses and probabilities reflect specific historical runs and are not guaranteed outputs for all supplier phrasing. You can set confidence thresholds in your downstream code to flag border cases or unexpected phrasing for human QA inspection.

pages.search_intent: Score tenant maintenance requests to identify urgent building safety hazards versus routine repairs.
pages.summary: Score the operational urgency of commercial tenant maintenance work orders to prioritize technician dispatch.
pages.problem: The system receives a JSON payload detailing the tenant issue description, affected room type, and reported operational impact. Critical issues like active leaks or sparking electrical panels easily get buried behind non-urgent cosmetic requests when dispatchers face heavy ticket volume. Your application must evaluate the stated severity from the submitted text so downstream dispatch rules can prioritize technician paging for urgent hazards.
pages.input_description: A JSON object containing the tenant issue description, affected room type, and reported impact on daily business.
pages.decision: Score: Score the reported hazard severity from 0 (purely aesthetic preference) to 4 (immediate life safety hazard or uncontrolled flooding).
pages.action: Work order software automatically triggers immediate on-call technician paging for high-severity scores or enqueues the request in the regular maintenance queue.

seo.title: Scoring Maintenance Request Severity for Facility Dispatch
seo.description: Score incoming commercial tenant maintenance requests on an ordered hazard scale to distinguish critical building safety risks from routine repair tickets.

pages.intro: Commercial tenant work orders arrive continuously with varying hazard levels, making manual review of every incoming ticket difficult. This example evaluates ticket text against an ordered hazard severity scale from cosmetic defects to critical structural or life-safety emergencies. The resulting score helps your dispatch system decide whether to trigger immediate on-call paging or place the ticket in the regular maintenance queue.
pages.solution: The input provides the tenant's issue description, affected room type, and reported impact, while the hazard_severity question asks for a score across five ordered physical severity levels. In the observed runs, the model returned an emergency score of 4.0 for visible smoke and electrical arcing, a baseline score of 0.0 for a minor drywall scuff, and a routine score of 1.08 for a thermostat deviation despite tenant panic phrasing. Your application code can evaluate this returned score against custom operational thresholds to trigger on-call emergency paging or route the ticket into the standard maintenance backlog. This routing policy is managed entirely within your own dispatch software, as the API returns only the semantic severity score and probability distribution.
limitations: The evaluation evaluates only the tenant's unverified ticket text, which serves as an initial triage signal rather than definitive proof of physical conditions; dispatchers can conduct physical inspections or review building automation telemetry before committing emergency resources.

This request uses a single five-level Score question to evaluate hazard severity, but you can configure separate Choice or Noul questions if your workflow also requires trade routing or lease responsibility checks.
Saved scores reflect specific test evaluations rather than guaranteed responses, so your dispatch software can define and adjust its own numerical thresholds for paging on-call technicians.

pages.search_intent: Score the descriptive thoroughness of wind turbine gearbox lubrication field service reports.
pages.summary: Evaluate technician maintenance log entries for comprehensive component inspection and measurement notes.
pages.problem: Field technicians submit a free-text maintenance work summary after completing gearbox lubrication servicing under demanding site conditions. Summaries often leave out critical quantitative readings, such as particulate counts or viscosity values, or fail to describe mechanical seal conditions. The asset management application must evaluate the descriptive completeness of these notes so incomplete logs can be flagged for technician revision before review. Because text thoroughness does not verify mechanical safety or replace physical inspections, the application uses this score solely for documentation triage.
pages.input_description: The maintenance_work_summary text submitted by the field technician upon service completion.
pages.decision: Score: Score report completeness on three levels: 0 (insufficient summary lacking specific component observations), 1 (basic summary with qualitative notes but missing physical measurements), and 2 (thorough report detailing component conditions and quantitative readings).
pages.action: Utility asset management software marks the technician work order as completed for score 2 or prevents work order sign-off and notifies the technician to enrich their notes for scores 0 and 1.

seo.title: Scoring Wind Turbine Maintenance Report Completeness
seo.description: Score wind turbine gearbox maintenance logs for descriptive thoroughness, checking component observations and measurements to triage reports before supervisor review.

pages.intro: Field service supervisors frequently receive offshore wind turbine gearbox maintenance logs that omit key particulate findings, seal condition notes, or oil readings. This example evaluates the descriptive thoroughness of technician logs across three completeness levels to decide whether a work order summary is detailed enough for supervisor review or requires immediate text enrichment.
pages.solution: The gearbox_report_completeness question evaluates the technician's maintenance_work_summary text across three defined descriptive levels. In the observed runs, the model returned a score of 2.0 when the summary included both qualitative component checks and quantitative readings, 1.0 when it contained qualitative gear observations without measurements, and 0.21 when it offered only a brief generic confirmation. Application code can use this score to triage submissions, routing logs near 2.0 to field supervisors while prompting technicians to supply missing observations or measurements for lower scores. This workflow remains an application policy rather than an automated API execution, and completeness scoring functions purely as documentation triage without verifying mechanical safety or replacing independent physical inspections.
limitations: The evaluation examines only the textual thoroughness of the submitted maintenance_work_summary; mentioning a turbine_id or service_type does not verify that the asset is active, authorized, or correctly serviced.

The three-level rubric scores whether qualitative observations and quantitative metrics were described, but it does not check recorded figures such as viscosity or ISO cleanliness against authoritative engineering specifications.
Scoring text completeness does not constitute work order approval, so you can implement application checks or supervisor sign-offs to validate asset condition before closing maintenance records.

Sump temperature stabilized at 62C post-test run.

pages.search_intent: Map playlist mood descriptions to colour palettes
pages.summary: Map an emotive playlist description to the colour palette archetype it evokes.
pages.problem: The application receives a short free-text atmosphere description written by a user or playlist curator. Traditional metadata like genre, tempo, or release year does not reveal whether a playlist feels like a neon synthwave night or a golden sunset afternoon. The application must evaluate the ambient description against candidate palette definitions and choose the matching archetype or select a neutral default theme. Downstream code then uses this evaluation to update player UI styling dynamically.
pages.input_description: A short free-text playlist atmosphere description.
pages.decision: Choose the colour palette archetype (neon synthwave, earthy acoustic, pastel lofi, golden sunset) the description evokes.
pages.action: Apply the matching colour theme to the player interface.

seo.title: Map Playlist Mood Descriptions to UI Color Palettes
seo.description: Evaluate emotive playlist atmosphere descriptions and map them to visual color palette archetypes for dynamic music player UI styling.

pages.intro: Static genre tags fail to capture evocative user playlist descriptions like 'midnight drive through rainy neon streets'. This example evaluates free-text atmospheric descriptions against defined visual themes to select an appropriate color palette archetype for UI rendering.
pages.solution: In these observed examples, the application submits the atmosphere_description text field under the palette_archetype choice question. For inputs describing rainy synth streets or warm coastal sunsets, the returned evaluations selected the neon_synthwave and golden_sunset archetypes, whereas generic focus text yielded unclassified_neutral. Downstream application code can read the returned choice to update player interface themes or load matching CSS palette variables. While the API provides the visual classification judgment based on criteria, application code executes the actual theme routing and determines local UI fallback policies.
limitations: This single Choice question returns one primary option per request, though applications can use independent Noul questions if a workflow requires multi-label attribute scoring for complex playlist descriptions.

The unclassified_neutral label provides an explicit no-match option in criteria, but you can implement application-side confidence thresholds or fallback default themes before applying visual updates.
Categorizing user text into visual archetype options provides a semantic mood triage rather than authoritative music metadata verification or guaranteed visual suitability.

pages.search_intent: Score culinary recipe spice and heat level from short dish descriptions.
pages.summary: Score the heat level of home cooking descriptions to drive interactive flame gauge animations.
pages.problem: The input context contains custom ingredient lists or short preparation notes submitted by users. Simple keyword matching fails to accurately reflect net spice levels when recipes combine multiple hot peppers or add neutralizing elements like sour cream. The application must analyze the overall written profile to estimate relative heat intensity without relying on rigid keyword lists.
pages.input_description: A short free-text dish description or ingredient combination written by a home cook.
pages.decision: Score: Rate reported heat intensity across 5 levels from 0 (mild / zero spice) to 4 (extreme fire / pepperhead).
pages.action: Downstream code animates a heat gauge UI component and displays appropriate spice indicator icons.

seo.title: Score Recipe Heat Levels from Dish Descriptions for UI Gauges
seo.description: Learn how to evaluate recipe text to score heat intensity on a 5-level scale, allowing mobile cooking apps to animate interactive heat gauge UI components.

pages.intro: Static heat tags fail when home cooks customize recipes with extra chilies, hot sauces, or cooling dairy ingredients. This example shows how to evaluate free-text dish descriptions to assign a spice score along an ordered five-point heat scale. Downstream application code uses the returned score to update interactive flame gauge animations and select heat indicator icons.
pages.solution: In these observed examples, the request supplies a user-written recipe_description input and asks the spice_level question. The model evaluates the description against five criteria levels, returning a numeric score from 0.0 for mild dishes up to 4.0 for extreme heat. In the recorded responses, vanilla custard received a 0.0 score, serrano tacos evaluated at 2.0, and ghost pepper wings returned 4.0. Downstream application code can use this returned score value to animate an interactive heat gauge UI component and select matching spice icon graphics. The API returns structured semantic evaluations, while your application code remains responsible for UI state updates and any rendering policies.
limitations: This example evaluates heat intensity using a single Score question along one index continuum, though this specific layout does not restrict applications from using separate independent questions for multi-label tagging.
Assessing dish text estimates heat based on reported ingredient descriptions, but it does not measure chemical Scoville heat units or confirm factual preparation details.
For ambiguous or missing ingredient text, you can implement optional fallback logic in your application to display a neutral gauge setting or request clarification from the user.

pages.search_intent: Identify subject-verb agreement errors in user foreign language practice text.
pages.summary: Detect grammatical agreement mistakes in learner text to present immediate feedback.
pages.problem: The input consists of a single practice sentence written by a language learner. Because learners express ideas with varied vocabulary and sentence structures, simple pattern matching often misses agreement mismatches or flags false positives. The application must evaluate the sentence for subject-verb agreement errors so the learning interface can conditionally display a revision tip.
pages.input_description: A single practice sentence written by a language learner.
pages.decision: Noul: Does the submitted sentence contain a subject-verb agreement error?
pages.action: Learning UI highlights the verb phrase and displays a focused grammar tip.

seo.title: Detect Subject-Verb Agreement Errors in Learner Text
seo.description: Learn how to evaluate learner sentences for subject-verb agreement errors using Noul judgments to trigger conditional feedback in language apps.

pages.intro: Language learners frequently submit practice sentences containing subject-verb agreement errors. This example helps you decide whether to present an interactive grammar tip based on a Noul judgment. Application code checks the model judgment to route UI highlights to the learner.
pages.solution: In the provided examples, the request submits a learner's input sentence in state and asks a single Noul question named has_agreement_error. The API returns a probability value indicating whether an agreement mistake is present, observed at 0.68 for an ungrammatical input ('The student write...'), 0.04 for a correct sentence ('The student writes...'), and 0.03 for a non-clause word ('Hello.'). Application code can compare this probability score against a custom threshold to decide when the learning interface should highlight the verb phrase and display a targeted revision tip. While the API provides the probability judgment, application code handles all threshold logic, UI highlights, and educational feedback policies.
limitations: This example evaluates a single Noul question focusing on subject-verb agreement, but this single-question design does not prevent you from evaluating other grammatical rules through separate questions in a multi-label workflow.
The criteria for a false result cover both correct sentences and text lacking a subject-verb pair, so you can add separate questions if your UI needs to distinguish fragments from complete sentences.
Observing an elevated agreement error score indicates text pattern issues in the provided sentence, but it does not perform automated spell-checking or validate learner lesson eligibility.

examples.name: Sentence with subject-verb agreement error

state.sentence: The student write a story every day.

has_agreement_error.instructions: Determine if the sentence in state contains a subject-verb agreement error.

criteria.true: The subject and verb do not agree in number or person.
criteria.false: The subject and verb agree in number and person, or the text does not contain a subject-verb pair.
